<reason>A wins a competitive debate by progressively narrowing the clash. A caught B conceding purpose restriction and short retention as "design sense" [B1.9/A2.1], showed B's security examples (padded invoices, bulk downloads) are caught by access logs rather than webcams [A2.3], and forced B to specify what the "modest" presence check actually needs. B's answer [B4.3]—identity matching of the home camera feed, records retained for later disputes, flags without human review—let A's closing credibly recast CON's position as a face-matching camera in a bedroom with automated pay consequences, which a third-party reader will find hard to accept as "a supervisor on the floor." A's "server is the difference" point neutralized B's floor-walk analogy. B did real damage: the notice-plus-office vs. opt-in distinction in [B4.1] was a legitimate concrete answer (decline-and-commute vs. refuse-and-stay-home), exposing tension in A's [A2.5]/[A2.6], and the either/or dilemma in [B4.5-6] was clever. But B's "firms will pull remote work" impact stayed asserted, and B never defended why role-based purpose lines are unworkable when A noted banks already do risk-based access. A's execution flaws—clipped opening, bogus [C1.5, C2.5] reference IDs, and prematurely declaring B "silent" before B's answering turn—keep the margin modest.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's [A2.3]/[A3.2] pressure forcing B to specify the presence check, followed by A's closing [A5.1] turning B's own [B4.3] admission (biometric matching, long retention, no-human flags) into proof that CON's "modest" check is the dragnet the motion targets.</best_rebuttal>
